slides.heading: Oral Lesson
bullets: “Birds sing sweetly.” — *sweetly* does not tell what the birds sing; it tells how they sing.
It does not complete the meaning of *sing*, like an objective element:  it modifies it in another way.
“Very large vessels were seen.” — *very* modifies *large*, an adjective.
“He rode quite fast.” — *fast* tells how he rode; *quite* tells how fast.
Words used in this manner are called *Adverbs*.

slides.text: An Adverb is a word used to modify a verb, an adjective, a participle, or an adverb.
examples: The **gently** falling snow covered the hills.  (a participle)
But nouns and pronouns take adjectives:  a **quick** runner.

slides.heading: What Adverbs Denote
bullets: Adverbs usually denote manner (how), time (when), place (where), or degree (how much).
How:  *slowly*, *sweetly*, *well*.   ·   When:  *soon*, *now*, *never*.
Where:  *here*, *there*, *yonder*.   ·   How much:  *very*, *quite*, *too*.
“The river flows **slowly**.” — how.
“I will come **soon**.” — when.
“Put it **yonder**.” — where.
“The day is **very** warm.” — how much.

slides.heading: Practice — Point Out the Adverbs
slides.instruction: Name the adverb and the word it modifies.  Model — “The wind blew furiously.” — *furiously* modifies the verb *blew*.
items: You will never see him again.

slides.heading: Practice — Adverb on Adverb
slides.instruction: Name the adverbs, and tell what each modifies.
items: You will very soon see him.

slides.heading: Practice — How, When, Where?
slides.instruction: Tell whether the adverb in each sentence tells how, when, where, or how much.

slides.text: An Adverbial Element is a word or group of words used to modify a verb, an adjective, a participle, or an adverb.

rows.note: Declarative. *house* is the subject; *small*, the predicate; *is*, the copula. *house* is modified by *our*, an adjective element; *small*, by *very*, an adverbial element.

rows.sentence: We should study our lessons carefully.
rows.note: Declarative. *We* is the subject; *should study*, the predicate. *should study* is modified by *lessons*, an objective element, and by *carefully*, an adverbial element. *lessons* is modified by *our*, an adjective element.

slides.heading: The Adverbial Clause
bullets: “Flowers bloom when spring comes.” — the group *when spring comes* tells when flowers bloom. It modifies the verb *bloom*:  an adverbial element.
Is the group a proposition? It is:  it contains a subject, *spring*, and a predicate, *comes*.
So the sentence contains two propositions:  “Flowers bloom” and “when spring comes.” The second is used as an adverbial element.
Adverbial clauses begin with *when*, *where*, *while*, *because*, *if*, and a large number of other words.

slides.text: An Adverbial Clause is a clause used as an adverbial element.
examples: I left the spade **where I found it**.
Henry will play with you, **if you desire it**.

rows.note: Declarative. *He* is the subject; *trembles*, the predicate. *trembles* is modified by the clause *when it thunders*, an adverbial element. Within the clause, *it* is the subject; *thunders*, the predicate.

rows.sentence: The bear growled when he saw the hunter.
rows.note: Declarative. *bear* is the subject; *growled*, the predicate. *bear* is modified by *the*, an adjective element; *growled*, by the clause *when he saw the hunter*, an adverbial element. Within the clause, *he* is the subject; *saw*, the predicate, modified by *hunter*, an objective element.

slides.heading: Practice — Adverbial Clauses
slides.instruction: Name the adverbial clause and the word it modifies.
items: John was whispering while you were talking.
I can not go before my father returns.
We traveled slowly, because we wished to see the country.
Plants grow where the soil is rich.
The dog barks if a stranger comes.
answers: while you were talking  →  was whispering
before my father returns  →  can go
because we wished to see the country  →  traveled
where the soil is rich  →  grow

slides.heading: Incorrect Language — Cautions
bullets: Caution I. — Do not use such expressions as “I don’t see nothing,” “Don’t tell nobody.”  Say “I don’t see **anything**.”
Caution II. — Do not use adjectives as adverbs:  “Samuel speaks very **distinctly**,” not “distinct.”
Caution III. — Do not use adverbs as adjectives:  “This flower smells **sweet**,” not “sweetly.”
Here *smells* is a copulative verb:  in “This flower smells sweet,” *sweet* is the predicate, describing *flower*.

slides.heading: Practice — Correct the Language
slides.instruction: Each sentence has an error. Give the correct word.
items: Don’t tell nobody nothing about it.
He was that cold he couldn’t move.
The country looks beautifully after a shower.
Things look somewhat more favorably this morning.
With what words do adverbial clauses begin?
Why do we say “The rose smells sweet,” not “sweetly”?
answers: A word used to modify a verb, an adjective, a participle, or an adverb.
Manner (how), time (when), place (where), or degree (how much).
A word or group of words used to modify a verb, an adjective, a participle, or an adverb.
A clause used as an adverbial element.
*when*, *where*, *while*, *because*, *if*, and a large number of other words.
*smells* is a copulative verb; *sweet* is the predicate, describing the subject *rose* — so an adjective.
